opening.argument: Judge, look at the combined solicitation signals. A video presented as Microsoft interview preparation leads its description with a low-cost hosting purchase link. The speaker endorses the hosting service, directs viewers to the description to buy, and also promises access to thousands of Microsoft questions through another link. Each statement is visible in isolation, but together they use an education-seeking audience to generate clicks and purchases. The educational material does not itself establish what viewers will encounter or receive after following those links.

opening.argument: Judge, the interview format also functions as a route into the speaker's own offerings. After telling viewers they can find thousands of Microsoft questions through a link, he asks them to subscribe for thousands of technical videos. Elsewhere he describes his company as providing training and internships and says viewers can contact him about its courses. Treat the educational presentation and the participation requests as one viewer journey when assessing the offer.

A viewer journey toward more content or disclosed paid training is not, on this evidence, a scam.
